from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('pages',len(r.pages))
text=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages,1):
 t=p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
 Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i:02d}.txt').write_text(t)
 text.append(f'\\n\\n========== PAGE {i} ==========\\n'+t)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(text))
print(''.join(text)[:62000])
PY"

strengths: AugSub provides a simple, practical training modification: shared weights and detached prediction targets allow stronger regularization without adding inference-time parameters or computation. The broad empirical support favors weak acceptance despite reservations about originality and mechanism.

ImageNet improvements are consistent across model sizes and training lengths. Table 3 reports gains of 0.6–0.7 percentage points after 400 epochs and 0.3–0.5 points after 800 epochs over DeiT-III. Table A.2 supports the core ViT-B improvement with results of 83.46±0.04 versus 84.08±0.02.

The evaluation extends meaningfully beyond one architecture or benchmark: MAE/BEiT/CLIP finetuning, ResNet, Swin, robustness, segmentation, detection, and transfer learning. Examples include ImageNet-A improving from 51.9 to 58.3 for ViT-H and ADE20K single-scale mIoU improving from 48.8 to 49.4 for ViT-B.

The paper explicitly evaluates additional training cost. In Table 6, ViT-B with AugMask achieves 84.1 accuracy in 25 GPU-days versus 83.7 in 26 GPU-days for longer baseline training, supporting usefulness beyond comparisons at equal epoch counts.

Reproducibility is supported by concise pseudocode, detailed training recipes in Appendix B, a stated code release, and three-run statistics for the principal ablations and transfer experiments. Using the same 50% masking ratio across recipes strengthens the practical applicability claim.
weaknesses: Originality relative to closely related consistency and self-distillation methods is insufficiently established. Section 2 acknowledges Co-sub but provides no direct experimental comparison, and dropout-consistency methods such as R-Drop are not addressed. The experiments establish improvement over base recipes more clearly than an advantage over the closest methodological alternatives.

The loss design lacks decisive controls. Table 1 does not compare against supervising both the original and dropped branches with ground-truth labels, or ablate the asymmetric stop-gradient design. Consequently, the specific contribution of relaxed targets is not isolated from retaining ordinary supervised training alongside an additional branch.

The proposed explanation overstates what the objective establishes. Equation 3 applies consistency supervision to every example, including confidently incorrect main-model predictions; it does not restrict regularization exclusively to successfully learned examples as claimed in Section 3.1. Figure 3 supports a weaker observation about average gradient magnitudes, rather than demonstrating the claimed sample-level prioritization.

Benefits have meaningful qualifications. Training costs increase approximately 1.5 times for token-dropping ViTs and twice for hierarchical architectures. Section 4.2 acknowledges no improvement in CLIP's best-checkpoint performance, while Table 10 shows ViT-B CIFAR-100 accuracy falling from 91.9 to 89.6 when AugMask is also used during finetuning. These results limit the broad claims of consistently beneficial additional regularization.

Uncertainty reporting is uneven. Although the appendix strengthens the core results, the 0.1-point BEiT-v2 gains and 0.2/0.3-point COCO gains lack corresponding repeated-run estimates. These smaller improvements provide weaker evidence than the main ImageNet results.
